newsitem.title: USA: Clinton keeps sides guessing in airline dispute.
newsitem.headline: Clinton keeps sides guessing in airline dispute.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday refused to tip his hand on possible intervention in the American Airlines labour dispute and a federal mediator said as the clock ticked toward a midnight strike deadline there was no sign Clinton was preparing to act.
"I have no reason to believe that a presidential emergency board has been arranged." Kenneth Hipp, chairman of the National Mediation Board, told reporters at mid-afternoon.
Hipp said the talks had reached a "critical" phase.

Earlier, Clinton urged the parties to strike a deal. "They have a few more hours of work to do," he said, looking at his watch, when a reporter covering an unrelated White House ceremony asked if he would act to prevent the grounding of the nation's second largest airline.
The president met later with White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles and deputy White House counsel Bruce Lindsey, his point man on the issue, to get an update on the situation.

His non-committal remarks were in keeping with White House silence on options as a federal mediator went down to the wire in trying to help American and its pilots union agree on a new contract before midnight Friday (0500 GMT Saturday), when the pilots had threatened a walkout.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry set the tone for the day earlier by telling reporters he would have no comment whatsoever on what Clinton might decide to do. Later he said the president was not taking the strike lightly.
"The president has heard from many concerned individuals, and obviously, he is concerned himself. But we will continue to watch the negotiations closely," McCurry said.

"It would be prudent for these parties to resolve a difficult labour dispute through negotiation at the table, through the bargaining that they are doing using the services of the National Mediation Board. And again, the White House calls on these parties to settle their dispute so we can avoid a major disruption in our air transportation system."
The dispute put Clinton in a politically ticklish position since labour is a key constituency of his Democratic Party.
"We never agree with taking the strike weapon out of the hands of workers," said an American Federation of Labour official when asked how the unions would view intervention.

Clinton angered the labour movement during his first term by pressing for congressional approval of the North American Free Trade Agreement. But the AFL-CIO official, who asked not to be identified, said her organisation was unlikely to equate intervention in the airline row with the NAFTA controversy.
In 1993, Clinton successfully pressured American Airlines Chairman Robert Crandall into accepting binding arbitration after the airline's flight attendants walked off the job.
Under the Railway Labour Act, which also covers airlines, Clinton can declare a national emergency to stop a strike and keep planes flying for up to 60 days during arbitration.
If the parties agreed to accept the result, they would be bound by the arbitrator's ruling. If not, the pilots would then be free to strike or the airline to lock them out.
Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, a Republican from Texas -- home of the airline's headquarters in Fort Worth-Dallas -- was among those urging Clinton to block a strike.

"I've urged him to look at the powers he has and to see what the impact is on our area of the country and several other areas of the country and be ready to kick in, if something doesn't happen today," Hutchinson said on CNN.

Clinton "is saying, let the parties keep working, and I agree with the president -- he's doing what I would do -- because of course we all would like this to be settled in the free market. But he is also keeping his options very, very open," the senator said.

A unit of AMR Corp, American is the second largest U.S. air carrier. An economic impact report prepared by the Transportation Department on Thursday estimates that a shutdown of the airline by its 9,000 pilots would cost the U.S. economy up to $200 million a day.
